Einstein's career was marked by his use of visualized thought experiments, such as chasing beams of light, moving trains, and falling elevators, to understand physical problems and explain his ideas. Unlike physical experiments, thought experiments produce no new empirical data; they work as logical arguments framed in imaginary scenarios, and a good one can always be restated as a sound argument. Einstein's childhood thought experiment about chasing a light beam, which conflicted with his sense that the laws of optics should obey the principle of relativity, was a key step toward special relativity.

*In Love and Death* is the second studio album by American rock band the Used, released on September 28, 2004, and it became their most commercially successful release, earning platinum certification in the United States. Its title and music reflect the tragedies surrounding vocalist Bert McCracken during production, most notably the death of his pregnant ex-girlfriend Kate, to whom the album is dedicated. The album followed the band's self-titled 2002 debut and was supported by singles such as "Take It Away," "All That I've Got," and "I Caught Fire," along with tours and a cover of "Under Pressure" with My Chemical Romance.

The document traces the development of Mexican nationality law, which is governed chiefly by Article 30 of the Constitution and combines the principles of jus soli and jus sanguinis, with citizenship treated as a separate concept from nationality. Its history runs from the first constitutional definitions of 1836 through the 1857 and 1917 constitutions, showing how rules on women's nationality changed over time, from automatic derivation from husbands to later reforms such as the 1934 law that stopped marriage to a foreigner from automatically costing a woman her nationality. The text also notes that the period included discriminatory immigration circulars targeting various racial and ethnic groups.

Joseph Ganim, a Democrat and former attorney, served as mayor of Bridgeport, Connecticut from 1991 to 2003, when he resigned after being convicted on federal corruption charges, including racketeering, extortion, and bribery. He later mounted a political comeback, was elected mayor again in 2015, and has since been reelected to serve a seventh term. His tenure included major redevelopment projects such as The Ballpark at Harbor Yard and Webster Bank Arena, though he also personally profited through kickbacks from developers.

The Norwegian Special Operations Commando (NORSOC, Forsvarets spesialkommando) is a Norwegian Armed Forces special operations unit founded in 1982 in response to terrorist threats against interests such as North Sea oil platforms, and it was combined with the Naval Special Operations Commando under a joint command in 2014. The unit's roots trace to Norwegians serving with British special forces in the Second World War, and it was publicly acknowledged only gradually after decades of official secrecy, later taking part in operations in Kosovo, Afghanistan (including Task Force K-Bar and police training in Kabul), and hostage rescues. Entry requires passing a demanding general selection, a three-week SOF selection, and a year of basic training.

"Birthday Cake" is a sexually explicit R&B track by Rihanna from her 2011 album Talk That Talk, originally released as a one-minute-18-second interlude after fan demand led to its inclusion. A full-length remix featuring Chris Brown premiered in February 2012, peaked at number 24 on the Billboard Hot 100, and was certified two-times platinum by the RIAA. Critics were divided on the song, with many praising its provocative content while noting it was too short or designed as filler.

Durgapur is a major industrial hub and planned urban agglomeration in West Bengal, India, known for steel production, train wheel manufacturing, and an emerging IT sector, and nicknamed the "Steel Backbone of Industrial Bengal." Located on the northern bank of the Damodar River in Paschim Bardhaman district, it has a transitional climate with extremely hot summers, heavy monsoon rains, and cold, dry winters. The city is governed by the Durgapur Municipal Corporation, has a population of about 581,000 (2011 census) that is predominantly Hindu and Bengali-speaking, and its economy is driven by public sector units, engineering and chemical industries, and its proximity to the Raniganj coalfields.

El Salvador leads Central America in geothermal energy and has 1,312 MW of installed capacity as of 2006, split between thermal, hydroelectric, and geothermal sources, with most generation privately owned apart from hydroelectric. The government's 2007 National Energy Strategy and related policies aim to diversify the energy mix toward renewables, meet demand growth of roughly 5% annually, and reduce dependence on oil, supported by new incentives like the 2007 Fiscal Incentives Law. Electrification has risen to 83.4%, and the country is pursuing rural expansion and regional grid integration through the SIEPAC project.

Joseph Ganim is a Democratic politician and former attorney who served as mayor of Bridgeport, Connecticut from 1991 to 2003, when he resigned after being convicted on federal corruption charges, including bribery and racketeering. He made a political comeback, winning election again in 2015 and being reelected in 2019 and 2024, and he twice unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for governor of Connecticut. During his time as mayor he was credited with cleaning up the city's East End and redeveloping its waterfront, but he also collected kickbacks from developers, for which he was sentenced to nine years in prison.

The Sherbrooke Fusilier Regiment was a Canadian armoured regiment formed in 1940 from two Militia units in Sherbrooke, Quebec, and converted to armour in 1942 as the 27th Armoured Regiment. It fought in Normandy from D-Day onward, including the Authie battle, the Orne crossings, and the advance into Caen, where its commander Mel Gordon's tank was among the first into the city. Its armoured lineage continues today through the reserve regiment, The Sherbrooke Hussars.

Robert Wilson McCoy (1902–1961) was an American illustrator and painter best known as the second artist on the comic strip The Phantom, taking over from original artist Ray Moore in 1941 and remaining on the strip until he fell ill in 1961. Born in Troy, Missouri, he began his career as an errand boy at a St. Louis advertising agency, went on to produce commercial art such as billboards, magazine covers, and advertisements, and studied at several art schools, including Washington University. Known for his adventurous spirit and world travels, he researched the Mbuti pygmies in the Congo for The Phantom, which inspired the Bandar tribe in the strip's stories.

Dale Abbey, also known as the Abbey of Stanley Park, was a religious house near Ilkeston in Derbyshire, whose foundation legend traces its origins to a hermitage in the early 12th century. It was constituted as a Premonstratensian abbey in 1204, grew to hold numerous small properties, granges and parish churches, and by 1536 its income had fallen below the threshold for dissolution, allowing it to survive until 1538 after paying a fine. The chronicle of its founding, written by Thomas de Muskham in the mid-13th century, blends legend, banditry and local aristocratic history to explain how the community came to be established at Deepdale.

Komi Can't Communicate is a Japanese manga by Tomohito Oda, serialized in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 2016 to 2025 and collected in 37 volumes, following high school student Shoko Komi, who has severe social anxiety and sets out with her classmate Hitohito Tadano to make 100 friends. Critics generally praised its humor and compassionate handling of social anxiety, though some criticized its portrayal of a gender-fluid character.

James Macpherson (1736–1796) was a Scottish writer, poet, and politician best known for the Ossian cycle of epic poems, which he claimed to have translated from ancient Gaelic sources. Although his Gaelic translations were challenged as authentic by Irish scholars and Samuel Johnson, the question of authenticity remained debated long after his death. Later in life, Macpherson became a politician and government pamphleteer, sitting in Parliament from 1780 and writing defences of British policy, including a response to the American Declaration of Independence.

George Awsumb (1880–1959) was a Norwegian-American architect whose eclectic portfolio, spanning neoclassical, Gothic Revival, Prairie School, and International Style designs, emphasized grand public buildings and places of worship, many of them still in use and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Born in Norway and raised in Wisconsin, he trained in Chicago, toured Europe, and in 1919 moved to Memphis, Tennessee, where he designed landmarks such as the Memphis Municipal Auditorium and Idlewild Presbyterian Church. His sons and grandson carried on the family architectural legacy, contributing significantly to Memphis's development.

Yatterman is a Japanese anime series produced by Tatsunoko Productions, broadcast from 1977 to 1979 across 108 episodes, and it was the last show overseen by company founder Tatsuo Yoshida before his death. The story follows the teenage heroes Gan and Ai, who become the masked Yatterman-1 and Yatterman-2 and use mechanical creations, including the dog-shaped robot Yatterwan, to stop the villainous Doronbo gang from seizing the scattered Skull Stone pieces. Unlike earlier Time Bokan entries, it avoids time travel, instead parodying real places and figures through misspelled names, and the series has since spawned a 2008 remake, a 2009 live-action film, and the 2015 spin-off Yatterman Night.

The Tour de Ski is an annual cross-country skiing stage race held since the 2006–07 season, typically with six to nine stages in late December and early January across the Czech Republic, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland, and it usually concludes in Val di Fiemme with a steep final climb up Alpe Cermis. Created through a collaboration between Vegard Ulvang and Jürg Capol of FIS, the event combines varied formats such as sprints, mass starts, and pursuits, with overall standings determined by cumulative times and bonus seconds, alongside sprint and climbing classifications. Its inaugural edition drew mixed reactions from athletes and the press, but it grew into a major fixture of the World Cup, with dominant riders like Justyna Kowalczyk and Dario Cologna and later milestones such as Jessie Diggins becoming the first non-European overall winner.

These women were referred to by many derogatory terms such as "Yankee princess" and "Yankee whore," and were viewed as the lowest social class even as the Korean government praised them as "dollar-earning patriots" and the industry contributed significantly to the economy. The institutionalized system was shaped by Japanese colonial rule, U.S. military policy, and postwar poverty, and its scale fluctuated with the number of American troops stationed in the country.
